The Tao Te Ching, or Daodejing, is a foundational text of Taoism. Attributed to the sage Laozi and composed around the fourth to sixth century BCE, this short, poetic work describes the Tao—the way—the underlying principle of all existence, and how to live in harmony with it.

Just 81 brief chapters make up this work, containing around 5,000 words total, which makes it one of the most concise major philosophical texts. It is attributed to Laozi, literally meaning old master, though his historical existence remains debated; some scholars view him as legendary.

The text is written in Classical Chinese aphorisms and paradoxes that resist single interpretation. Countless commentaries exist because the core concept—the Tao is ineffable, beyond language and logic—creates this interpretive necessity. Those who speak of it do not know it, and those who know it do not speak. This paradox sits at the heart of Taoist thought.

The teaching emphasizes wu wei, non-action or action without force, flowing with natural patterns rather than imposing will. The text does this through feminine imagery of valley, water, and emptiness, while critiquing rigid Confucian morality and social hierarchy. The Tao Te Ching profoundly influenced Chinese philosophy, art, martial arts, and medicine. It also shaped Zen Buddhism in East Asia. The opening line captures its essence: the Tao that can be spoken of is not the eternal Tao. Laozi, as the traditional author, represents a philosophical counterweight to Confucius, and his work later merged with Buddhist thought to create Chan Buddhism.
